title: Numerical Algorithms: GCD, Modular Arithmetic, and Check Digits

questions.question: An agent types a beneficiary account number and swaps two adjacent digits. Which property of the identifier would let the form reject it before submission?
options: The account number is stored as a 64-bit integer rather than a string
The identifier carries a check digit computed so that transpositions break an equation
The bank publishes a list of all valid account numbers for lookup
The number is long enough that a random typo is unlikely to collide
questions.explanation: A check digit makes the whole identifier satisfy an equation (a weighted sum mod 10, the number mod 97, a table fold ending at 0) that most keying errors violate. Length alone does not help: a transposition of a valid number is another plausible number. Lookups are not available at form time and are what the check digit avoids.

questions.question: Why does Luhn catch every single-digit substitution but not the adjacent transposition 09 <-> 90?
options: Because the doubled-position map is a permutation of the digits, but 0 and 9 are the two digits it leaves unchanged
Because 0 and 9 are both treated as zero by the digit-sum step, so they are indistinguishable everywhere
Because Luhn only examines the odd positions and 0 and 9 happen to fall on even ones
Because the check digit is computed modulo 10 and 0 + 9 is congruent to 9 modulo 10
questions.explanation: The doubled map sends 0..9 to 0,2,4,6,8,1,3,5,7,9, a permutation, so any single change alters the sum. A transposition swaps which digit is doubled, changing the sum by (f(a) - a) - (f(b) - b); f(d) - d is zero only for d = 0 and d = 9, so only that pair is invisible. 0 and 9 are perfectly distinguishable as single digits.

questions.question: The IBAN DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00 is checked by computing a 24-digit number modulo 97. The Java and Go versions do this in a long without overflow. How?
options: They parse the number with BigInteger-style arbitrary precision and then reduce once
They reduce modulo 97 after every digit, so the running value never exceeds 10 * 97 + 9
They split the IBAN into two 12-digit halves and combine the remainders
They use floating point, which has enough precision for 24 significant digits
questions.explanation: Horner's rule evaluates r = (r * 10 + digit) mod 97 left to right; r stays below 97 so the intermediate is at most 979. The 24-digit number is never formed. Splitting into halves also works but needs the weight 10^12 mod 97; a double has only about 16 significant digits and would be wrong.

questions.question: Damm's check digit folds digits through a 10 x 10 table. Which property of the table guarantees that every adjacent transposition is detected?
options: Every row and every column of the table is a permutation of the digits 0 through 9
The main diagonal of the table is all zeros, so appending the state returns to zero
Total anti-symmetry: T[T[c][x]][y] differs from T[T[c][y]][x] whenever x differs from y
The table is symmetric about its main diagonal, so T[x][y] always equals T[y][x]
questions.explanation: Total anti-symmetry says exactly that feeding x then y from any state c reaches a different state than feeding y then x, which is what makes a swap of neighbours visible. The Latin-square property (rows and columns are permutations) is what guarantees single-digit errors; the zero diagonal is what lets the check digit drive the final state to 0. The table is not symmetric.

questions.question: A team tests its Luhn implementation by flipping one random digit a thousand times and reports 100% detection. Which real keying error class is their test blind to, and what does Luhn actually do with it?
options: Twin errors (aa -> bb); Luhn detects all of them because doubled and undoubled digits sum differently
Jump transpositions (digits two apart swapped); Luhn detects none of them because the two positions carry the same weight
Adjacent transpositions; Luhn detects none of them because its weights alternate between the two positions
Single-digit errors in the check position itself; Luhn ignores the check digit when it validates a number
questions.explanation: Positions two apart are both doubled or both undoubled, so swapping them leaves the sum unchanged: the aggregate run shows 0 of 2,531 jump transpositions caught. Luhn catches most adjacent transpositions (all but 09/90) and most twin errors (all but three pairs). A single-random-flip test can never surface a weakness in transpositions, which is why the lesson enumerates each class exhaustively.

questions.question: A new internal reference number is digits only and has room for exactly one check digit. It must catch every single-digit error and every adjacent transposition. Which choice meets the requirement?
options: Luhn, because it is the card-industry standard and catches every single-digit error
ISO 7064 MOD 97-10, truncated to its first check digit to fit the field
Damm or Verhoeff, whose table-based folds guarantee both classes with a single digit
A CRC-8 over the digit string, which detects all single-bit and burst errors
questions.explanation: Damm and Verhoeff are designed for precisely these two guarantees in one digit; Luhn misses the 09/90 transposition and cannot be fixed within one digit. Truncating MOD 97-10 destroys its arithmetic guarantees. A CRC models bit errors on a wire, not a human swapping two digits, and gives no proven coverage of transpositions.
